introduction: “Sometimes joking is necessary. Otherwise we would get depressed.” This guide is largely stories: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá teasing His correspondents and secretaries, jokes He told about pompous theologians, flattering courtiers, quarrelling sectarians and a philosopher cow, and memories of His laughter in prison and on His travels; a few readings say why it matters, that humour is “the salt of conversation” and that seriousness “clothed in the garment of humor” goes deeper. The Bible laughs more than its reputation suggests: Sarah, the Psalmist whose mouth was filled with laughter, Proverbs’ sluggard and haggler, Jesus’s camel swallowed and beam in the eye, Rhoda leaving Peter at the gate. Aristotle made ready wit a virtue between buffoonery and boorishness; Shakespeare, Swift, Dickens, Twain and Chesterton supply fellow jesters. The cautions are also here: Ephesians against jesting, Ben Sira’s wise man who “doth scarce smile”, Proverbs on the man who wounds and says “Am not I in sport?”, and Elijah’s mockery, which did not end in laughter.
questions: Which of these stories made you laugh? What, exactly, was funny, and at whose expense?

Reading 20 prefers “pure seriousness clothed in the garment of humor”. Take one of the told jokes (the theologian at sea, the eggplant, the three men in the boat) and state its serious point. What does the joke do that the statement does not?
Aristotle places wit between buffoonery and boorishness. Where do the readings draw the same two boundaries?
Several stories mock clergy and the learned. What keeps such satire from the fault Proverbs names, “Am not I in sport?”
Ephesians lists jesting among things “not convenient”, and Ben Sira’s wise man hardly smiles. How do you reconcile such texts with a holy figure who laughed heartily?
What is the difference between laughing with someone and laughing at them, in the letters of stretches two and three?

outside.why: “Sometimes joking is necessary. Otherwise we would get depressed.” A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones.
Two hours in every twenty-four to be spent in happiness. A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance.
A broken telegraph wire to heaven, and the answer: use wireless. Chesterton: a characteristic of the great saints is their power of levity. Angels can fly because they can take themselves lightly.
Grieve not that the Tablet is brief. Polonius, at length: since brevity is the soul of wit, I will be brief.
“Joking is the salt of conversation.” Paul uses the same figure: let your speech be always with grace, seasoned with salt.

Aristotle counted ready wit among the virtues, a mean between two faults: those who carry humour to excess are thought to be vulgar buffoons, while those who can neither make a joke themselves nor put up with those who do are thought to be boorish and unpolished.
The Prophet was fond of jest, so there is no harm in it. The Qur’an: He it is who maketh laugh, and maketh weep.

The New Testament has a sterner sentence: neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient: but rather giving of thanks. Much Christian piety took it as a rule against levity. What kind of jesting do you think it has in view, and would the humour of these readings fall under it?
At luncheon He asks whether the pilgrims are happy. A feast is made for laughter, and wine maketh merry.

Give the poor more than words, or their pockets will be none the fuller. James makes the same joke in earnest: if one of you say unto them, Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled; notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful; what doth it profit?
A pasha who was “a mountain of pride” and set up gallows wherever he went. He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh: the Lord shall have them in derision.
An hour each evening of stories and pithy remarks with the household. He that is of a merry heart hath a continual feast.
Playful letters to a companion in hardship. Byron: and if I laugh at any mortal thing, ’tis that I may not weep.
“This time will pass.” Till he fill thy mouth with laughing, and thy lips with rejoicing.
It is pleasant to joke with a friend who has given away even the ruins of his house. A merry heart goes all the day, your sad tires in a mile-a.
Teasing congratulations on a son. Sarah, at the birth of a child named Laughter: God hath made me to laugh, so that all that hear will laugh with me.
Humour that is “pure seriousness clothed in the garment of humor” works more deeply. Nathan brought a king to judge himself with a story about a poor man’s one little ewe lamb.
Shakespeare’s clown states the principle: better a witty fool, than a foolish wit.

A pen that has been “bowing and prostrating since morning”: comedy in the middle of sacred work. The book of Acts has a moment of it at a prayer meeting: Rhoda knew Peter’s voice, and opened not the gate for gladness, but ran in to tell them. Why would a scripture keep such a detail?
A correspondent waiting “like an unrelenting creditor” for his letter. Jesus tells of one who gets his loaves at midnight because of his importunity.
“Each day, by some device, you exact from me a toll.” The widow and the judge: because this widow troubleth me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me.

Friends who write to ask Him to cough and sneeze for them. Franklin’s joke at his own expense is of the same dry kind: even if I could conceive that I had completely overcome pride, I should probably be proud of my humility.
A secretary who writes down every joke, to be spread everywhere. A jest’s prosperity lies in the ear of him that hears it, never in the tongue of him that makes it.
“O usurper of this servant’s right!”: a mock quarrel over who shall be the servant. Whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant.
A playful demand for an ode in “utter lowliness”. When thou art bidden, go and sit down in the lowest room.
One person triumphing over two hundred, told with a smile. How many a little company hath overcome a mighty host by Allah’s leave!
He stood laughing to His heart’s content. Then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing.

The theologian who told the captain half his life was lost for want of theology, and could not swim. Dickens’s schoolmaster is the same man: now, what I want is, Facts. Teach these boys and girls nothing but Facts.
Paul’s six words on the theologian’s complaint, written to a learned and quarrelsome congregation: knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth.

“I am your servant and not the servant of an eggplant.” A messenger coaches the prophet Micaiah: the prophets declare good unto the king with one mouth; let thy word be like theirs. He answers: what the Lord saith unto me, that will I speak.
A man who vowed to sell his camel for a penny and found a way round the vow. Market comedy from Proverbs: it is naught, it is naught, saith the buyer: but when he is gone his way, then he boasteth.
A gossip who claims to follow God’s example in mentioning Adam’s sin. The mote in thy brother’s eye and the beam in thine own: Jesus’s comic exaggeration on the same subject.

The Kurd who interrupts his prayer to tell admirers he is fasting too. When thou prayest, thou shalt not be as the hypocrites are: for they love to pray standing in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen of men.
A pupil caught out, in a cloud of smoke. Proverbs draws its idler like a cartoon: there is a lion in the way; as the door turneth upon his hinges, so doth the slothful upon his bed.

A mullah answers one verse with another to avoid a question. He cites the principle behind this saying: neither cast ye your pearls before swine. The story laughs at him for it. When is that verse wisdom and when is it an excuse?
“Like entrusting meat to a cat”: a fable in a phrase. Aesop’s method at full length: the Wind blew and the traveller wrapped his cloak closer; the Sun shone, and he took it off.

A minister asks with what ladder a heavy man ascended to heaven, and is answered in kind. Religious mockery has a prophet for precedent: Elijah mocked them, and said, Cry aloud: for he is a god; either he is talking, or he is in a journey, or peradventure he sleepeth. Elijah’s contest ended in slaughter. What keeps wit in religious argument from becoming contempt?
Three men in a boat, two praying for each other’s drowning. Swift: we have just enough religion to make us hate, but not enough to make us love one another.
Disciples propose to call down fire on a village of another sect: ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of.
A dog beaten for defiling a seminary that an intelligent man never enters. Ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel.

A verse on the glutton mullah. Chaucer, who mocks his friar and pardoner, draws one poor parson straight: first he wrought, and afterward he taught. Does satire of the clergy need such a figure beside it to be fair?
“Her highness the Cow” as the perfect materialist. Twain reverses the comparison to the same end: man is the only animal that blushes. Or needs to.
If only the sensible is real, the cow is the supreme philosopher. Puck’s view from outside: Lord, what fools these mortals be!
People who study, work, walk and eat for dress. Consider the lilies of the field: even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these.
Soldiers as prisoners of their rules. Jaques’s soldier: full of strange oaths, seeking the bubble reputation even in the cannon’s mouth.
A dinner in Paris at a pound a head, told as comedy. Go thy way, eat thy bread with joy, and drink thy wine with a merry heart.
A proud king, a frightened court and a physician. The wrath of a king is as messengers of death: but a wise man will pacify it.
Officials who, hearing the Shah is dead, arrest whoever is at hand. Edmund on how people explain their disasters: this is the excellent foppery of the world.

A man keeps demanding the other cheek, day after day, until the joke turns. The saying itself: whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also. What does the story suggest about people who quote a precept for their own advantage?

Proverbs on where joking stops: as a mad man who casteth firebrands, arrows, and death, so is the man that deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport? Which stories in this guide come nearest that line?
A poor believer who entertained every new arrival. Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
A wood-chopper and wit, beaten, who has the last word. Falstaff, rising from the battlefield: the better part of valour is discretion.
An ant on a poplar tries to shake it, and the tree laughs. Behold, the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance.

“Lydia, Lydia, you cannot put up with this one man, and I have to put up with the whole human race.” The same doubled name and gentle reproof: Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things.

Ben Sira would have disapproved of most of this guide: a fool lifteth up his voice with laughter; but a wise man doth scarce smile a little. The readings show ‘Abdu’l-Bahá laughing aloud, often. What is the case for each view of holiness?

And Jesus has a hard word too: woe unto you that laugh now! for ye shall mourn and weep. He says in the same breath, of those who weep now, ye shall laugh. Whose laughter is being warned, and whose promised?

shortfall: Most of the readings in stretches two to five and eight to ten are affectionate personal letters and travellers’ anecdotes whose humour lies in their particulars; companions were given where a story has a moral or a known parallel, and the rest were left to be enjoyed as they are.
